sentences.text: Hey, Gary.
This meeting is being recorded.
You heard yourself?
Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
I'm very good.
Summer is finally feeling like it's on its way, at least swimming around the edge of the sky.
So feeling a little bit better about that because it's been raining solidly.
I don't know about how it's been in London, but it's.
Well, I'm in Belfast these days, so it's been pretty shitty, but it's.
It's nice here today, so mustn't grumble.
So, Andy, I'm not.
I'm not going to take up too much of your time.
So, long story short, as we.
We've discussed the.
The thing with Sophie, it's not really doable for the.
The reasons that you sort of presented to her and, and the research that we've done, but I'm still keen to exit.

Sophie's approach is for us to sit tight for like a couple of years, three years, and just try and build things up, you know, continue with improving on the EBITDA and increasing the revenue and stuff.

That's fine, you know, but, like, as you know, I'm no spring chicken and frankly, I've got other stuff that I want to crack on with, you know, I just wondered if it was worth us exploring, selling at less than what would be ideal for me, you know.
Or what would be less than ideal for you?
I think if I had, after.
After my.
The tax and divvy unite, all the bits, if I could.
If I could have like round about 600k in the bank, that would be.
That would be sufficient, I think so.
I'm not sure.
I've spoken to the accountant briefly about it, but I didn't get a firm figure from him on what that would actually mean.
But I think, because I think we were talking to you about 1.5 million and there's just no way we're going to get anywhere near that, you know.
So.
Okay.
So I just wonder what your thoughts are, if we should.
If we should indeed sit tight or if there would be a taker out there that we'd be willing to offer a decent amount, you know.
Yeah.
I would say my advice would be don't sit tight.
I think in these situations, Gary, what.
What tends to happen is businesses, agencies in particular service businesses, really start to lose their value when somebody is ready to sell.
You know, the potential is there for you to have worse and worse years.
So in three or four years could just be in a worse position.

You know, if you're kind of semi checked out and you want to, you want to sell then, then it's probably best you get to it as quickly as possible, get some offers on the table and see what the value is.
Yeah, if we get this out in the next year then there is still some entrepreneurs, relief to be had.
I think the, the rate is going up, isn't it?
They're trying to put the tax back up on that first 1 million that you can take out.
So there is still a good opportunity to get near six or roundabouts in into your account on day one and then potentially for, for another 600k to come in.
So usually we can get a 4x for agencies.
So I reckon around 1.2 would be doable.
600k up front, 600k later and maybe we'll get more, maybe we'll get more.
But, but the strategy tip to get 600k into your account, I think it's a pretty decent one.
It's doable.
That's it.
So in terms of how you want to go about that.
So we run two, two tiers of processes that are going to be suitable for you.
One is that we do a prep for market process which is basically evaluation and we build all the marketing materials that go with it.
The main thing that we need is what's called an im, an information memorandum.
And if we can, if we can get that, all the details, valuation and everything into a deck, we can set your listing up on agencies co and just get it out in front of our, in front of our market.
We've got 20,000 people signed up to that and there's a pretty good chance that in the first time that it goes out we generate enough interest to get a sale down.
So that's kind of like the, the least sort of risky and the quickest way to get to market, we do a sort of tier up above that which is a full M&A process.

And how it differs is when we have a client like yourself that kind of needs to just get out, it kind of guarantees that the process will run and we should get a buyer and a deal done within sort of a six month window and that's a little bit more expensive, it's 24k.
We break that into smaller payments.
But the initial payment is about 8k the first payment and then 4 of 4k.
So it's pricier.
But what it means is my team are working on your account every single day.

So particularly if that initial send out doesn't work, we also actually build a list of targets that aren't necessarily subscribers to agencies but we do know they've in this instance say they bought Shopify agencies before or they're in E Commerce etc etc so we would build up a, a list for potential buyers as well and my team then are working on that every single day to get buyers, you know, in, in a call with you and get that interest generated so we can get a deal done.
So I think that's the two flavors that we're looking at.
I don't know whether if either, either of those would suit you, but I think can you, can you send, send.
Us through in an email?
Would that be possible?
Yeah, sure, I can get that into an email with you.
But in either sense we either case, sorry, we would take 5%.
We would in the second instance the 24K, all of those retainer fees are actually netted out of the win fee.
Say we were to get 100k and you'd already paid 24 then you just pay the net out of your, out of your cash up front.
Yeah, I'll get them in, I'll get them in an email to you.
I mean the sooner we get up and running the better.
I would say, you know we can.
The, the kind of best time to sell to get started is around now.

It like I say it's usually about a six month process and if we can get it kind of done and dusted by around September, October because people start to lose their focus a little bit around November, particularly the Americans.
There's Thanksgiving and other stuff since November's are much slower.
And my feeling would be that we would want to get out all the way to the US as well because they've got more cash.
They're looking to offshore to the UK.
They like the creativity for you know, in UK companies etc.
So that, that's how I would, would see the opportunity for you to get out quickly.
Quick enough.
Gotcha.
And there's, there's one possible fly in the ointment.
So Sophie has been reworking the figures.

So she has been discussing pulling money from last financial year into this financial year to make things look a bit more stable because we had a, a decent last financial year which was sort of around about the 2.
250, 270 EBITDA.

I can't remember the figure but she wanted to pull some of that into this year because we had, we had a slow first few months of this financial year which starts in September and she thought that not going to be selling now, it would be better optics in A year or two to have a more modest 24 but a better 25.
So it's looking stable and moving in the right direction.
Do you.
Would you agree with that or do you think that's a bit of a.
It was a bit of a fiddle, isn't it?
I think most people are going to go through your books and they're going to see that kind of thing.
However, I think it would be accepted if you did actually deliver the work this year.
Otherwise, I think it's just a fudge.
And a lot of.
A lot of buyers are savvy enough to spot that was the work delivered this year.
Yeah.
So basically what we do is we take 50 upfront and then 30, then 20.
So a lot of the time we're sort of.
We're doing the work well after the, the, the first quarter of the engagement.
So it basically puts a lot of pressure on ourselves because it means that we're.
We're often.
We invoice for the money we don't get paid for, for the work until well into the engagement.
And we're also having to pay vat, so we're trying to rejig all of that.
So it's just a bit more manageable for us.
Cash is.
So we've got a new financial controller who's been helping us with that and she suggests.
She asked us why we were billing in the way we did because it was just punitive to ourselves.
So that sort of started the conversation about how it could make us look a bit healthier whenever the.
Things are a bit fallow, you know, so.
But I've got.
I've got figures prepped that I can share with you.
Anyway, that just explains that.
Yeah, yeah, I think, I think it's fine if you've delivered the work in, in the following financial year.
And it's.
I mean, that, that is.
I think it's kind of a doable thing you can do with HMRC as well, you know, moving cash around from different years.
As long as you're delivering the work, you've got somebody in the background if they want your attention.
So I think it, I think it's acceptable in that instance.
So, yeah, that's fine.
I mean, it does, it does still.
I mean, it doesn't really get you out of the hot water.
What, what, what really is the issue, Gary?
What.
Why are you not getting as much business as you used to do is maybe E commerce businesses are going in a different direction?
Or do you think there's something else that you're.
You're missing.

You can blame that on marketing or not closing.

So I, I still think Shopify's got legs, definitely.
And we are.
Things have just recently been.

So.

I've been.

Yeah, we've.

summary.overview: In the Business Strategy and Exit Planning meeting, Gary Carruthers expressed his urgency to exit the company, aiming for a net gain of £600k post-taxes, while Andy Day cautioned against delaying the sale due to potential decreases in business value. Andy outlined two exit strategies: preparing the company for market with necessary marketing materials or pursuing a full M&A process, with a preference for the latter to attract interested US buyers by September/October. Discussion turned to the company's recent underperformance, attributed to a poor sales pipeline and ineffective marketing efforts, particularly under Commercial Director Jordan’s leadership. Acknowledging a top-heavy management structure and a shift towards a more corporate culture, Andy suggested reassessing team roles and possibly cutting management positions to improve efficiency and save costs. They concluded that Gary should report back to Managing Director Sophie about team performance issues, share financial details with Andy, and decide on the next steps within two weeks, while Andy would follow up with the discussed process options.
summary.short_summary: Gary Carruthers expressed an urgent desire to exit the company with a target of £600k net gain post-taxes, while Andy Day warned that delaying the sale could diminish business value. He proposed two exit strategies: preparing for market with essential marketing materials or opting for a full M&A process, favoring the latter to draw in US buyers by September/October. The discussion highlighted the company's recent underperformance, linked to a weak sales pipeline and ineffective marketing under Commercial Director Jordan's leadership. To enhance efficiency, Andy suggested reassessing team roles and potentially reducing the top-heavy management structure. The meeting concluded with Gary tasked to report team performance issues to Managing Director Sophie, share financial information with Andy, and decide on next steps in two weeks, while Andy would follow up on the proposed exit strategies.
